id: October, Remembering the Ride No One Saw

I release The bug to a desert wind That is racing toward the sea, A brutal dryness in its wake. Fire in the hills everywhere.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Steel, That, The

outputs.L1:
**Steel Horses**

Steel horses nodding in the petroleum field are beasts
that suck the crude of earth.
They have lived here for as long as I can remember.

This moment, I catch the scent of wild incense—
heather, abducted by a desert wind,
its tangled growth concealing
the rain-carved ribs of the foothills.
Evening swallows the city,
fasting through late autumn.

Years ago, after hearing the tale
of a boy who lost both legs
while playing atop an oil pump,
I was dared to straddle one myself.
All my friends stood watching,
the Pacific behind me burning with dusk.
The brute lifted me toward the sky,
where I merged with the twilight,
a warm breeze cradling my back.
None of them noticed
the world had stopped to breathe.

When I looked again, they had vanished.
Nearby, in bushes flowering pink,
someone had found
the girl who'd been missing for weeks.
They stood in stunned silence, her body
already decomposing, while I rode on,
the slow, bucking animal beneath me.

Two months later, from that same pump,
a man dove—
an imperfect swan into night.
He landed in the dirt gully,
shattering the soft, white wings
he never possessed.

Today, I cup in my hand
an insect charged with lightning.
It flickers against
the hollow of my palm
as I raise it to my lips and whisper
a wish so simple
that by morning, I will have forgotten it.
I release the creature to a desert wind
racing toward the sea,
trailing a brutal dryness in its wake.

Fire in the hills, everywhere.
outputs.L2:
Here's a reimagined version of the poem:

Iron stallions bow endlessly
Across the oilfield, hungry creatures
Draining
The earth's black blood.
They've stood sentinel here
For all my remembered years.
Right now, a wild fragrance drifts to me:
Sage, stolen away by desert winds.
Its tangled growth conceals
The rain-etched bones of the hills below.
Dusk devours
The town, starving in late autumn.

Long ago, after the tale reached me
Of a boy who forfeited
Both his legs to a pump jack's motion,
Someone dared me to mount one myself.
My friends gathered to witness,
The Pacific Ocean igniting behind me in sunset flame.
The creature raised me toward heaven,
Where I became one with the fading light,
A gentle wind cradling my shoulders.
Not one of them noticed
The universe holding its breath.
When I turned back, they had vanished.

Close by, in bushes flowering pink,
Someone had discovered
The girl gone missing for weeks now.
They gathered in silent horror around
Her decaying form, while I continued
Riding the sluggish, thrashing beast.

Two months later, from that very pump,
A man leapt—
A broken, imperfect swan diving into darkness.
He crashed into the dirt below,
Shattering wings
Made of nothing but white bone and hope.

Today, I trap within my palm
A firefly, pulsing with captured lightning.
It dances
Against the hidden curve of my hand
As I lift it near my lips and whisper
A wish so plain and small
That dawn will erase it from memory.
I set the creature free
Into a desert wind
Rushing toward the ocean,
Carrying its harsh drought behind it.
Flames consume the hillsides everywhere.
outputs.L3:
# Steel Horses

The oil pumps have always been there, for as long as I can remember—steel horses grazing on the horizon, their heads bowing and rising in that eternal, mechanical rhythm, drawing crude from the earth's dark veins. As a child, I thought of them as living things, breathing iron and rust, their metal ribs groaning with each descent. They never tired. They never slept. Long before I understood what oil meant to the town, to the men who worked the fields, to the economy that kept us fed, I understood only that the horses moved, and that movement felt like a kind of life.

I was eight, maybe nine, when the dare came. Some older kid—I don't remember who anymore, only the shape of his dare, the challenge in his voice—told me to climb onto one of the pumps while it moved, to ride it like the beast it resembled. I remember hesitating, remember the story that had circulated through the neighborhood like a warning whispered between adults and children alike: a boy, a few towns over, had tried the same thing and lost his legs to the machine's indifferent motion, crushed beneath steel that did not know the difference between crude oil and human bone. The story should have stopped me. It didn't.

I climbed on anyway. And for a moment—just a moment—I was somewhere else entirely. The world tilted and rose and fell with the pump's rhythm, and I felt weightless, suspended between fear and something like joy, something transcendent, as though I had slipped out of my body and into the machine's ancient pulse. I don't know how long I stayed there, riding that dreamlike arc. Long enough, apparently, for something terrible to happen nearby, though I didn't know it at the time. Long enough for men to find the body of a missing girl, decomposing in a ditch not far from where I clung to the beast's rising and falling head. No one saw me. No one noticed the reckless, ecstatic thing I had done, because their eyes—their whole attention—had turned toward death, toward the smell of it, toward the terrible discovery that would consume the town for weeks. My small transgression, my brush with flight, vanished into the shadow of something far larger.

Months passed. The girl was buried, mourned, slowly folded into memory. And then, as if the oil pump demanded another offering, a man climbed to its highest point one evening and let himself fall—not toward safety, not toward escape, but downward, into the earth the machine had spent its whole existence drawing from. They called it a suicide, of course, though I remember thinking, even then, that there was something almost deliberate in its shape, something like a swan dive gone wrong, imperfect and human, arms outstretched into an unfamiliar element. The machine that had given me a taste of transcendence had taken, in its own way, a man's entire future.

Now, years later, I stand in the desert at dusk, watching the last light drain from the sky the way oil once drained from the ground. A firefly blinks nearby, and without thinking, I close my hand around it—gently, carefully—feeling its small pulse of light against my palm. I make a wish, quick and unformed, the kind of wish that dissolves before you can even name it, and then I open my fingers and let the firefly go. It rises into the wind, which carries with it the dryness of the desert and, somewhere far off, the memory of fire, drifting steadily toward the sea.

I think of the girl, of the man, of the boy who lost his legs, of the boy who once rode a steel horse and felt, for one impossible moment, alive in a way that has never quite returned. The wind does not answer. It only carries everything forward—the dust, the heat, the small photons of light—toward whatever waits at the water's edge, indifferent to memory, indifferent to loss, moving the way the pumps always moved: steady, relentless, and utterly without mercy.
outputs.L4:
# The Beast in the Field

We called it the beast, that iron horse
nodding endlessly into earth and out again,
its dark head bowing to something buried
we couldn't name—oil, maybe, or time itself
pumped up through veins of Texas clay.

I was nine when Dale dared me to ride it,
to climb the counterweight while it dipped low
and hold on through the rise, the whole machine
groaning like something half-alive, half-dead,
somewhere between a heartbeat and a grave.

The desert around us kept its secrets close.
Just weeks before, they'd found the Hutchins girl—
not found her, really, just the place she'd been,
a hollow in the brush, her bicycle
rusting sideways in a ditch of weeds.
Nobody said the word. We understood
enough to know the land could swallow things
and never give them back the way they came.

And Mr. Voss, who worked the rig at dawn,
had fallen from the derrick two years gone,
his boot catching wrong on a rung of frost—
they said he didn't make a sound at all,
just dropped like something folding into sleep.

I thought of him as I climbed onto the beast,
felt the machine's breath lift me toward the sky,
that strange communion of a boy and iron,
suspended for a moment between fear
and something close to flying, close to prayer.
The whole world tilted—sagebrush, sky, the scar
of black where lightning once had burned the field
clean down to bone, a wound that never healed
but wore its damage like a badge of light.

Up there I understood what I could not
have said in words: that death moves through the world
the way the pumpjack moves, patient and slow,
and childhood is the space between its breaths—
brief, luminous, already halfway gone.

When I came down, my palms were black with grease,
my heart still hammering its small refrain.
I made a wish then, foolish as they come,
released it like a match struck in the wind
above that scorched and salt-white stretch of ground
where nothing but the derricks seemed to last,
where even memory bends and rusts and falls
into the dark the way that girl once did,
the way that man once did, the way we all
eventually surrender to the field's
slow appetite, its endless nodding prayer.

The beast kept pumping long after I left,
long after Dale moved on, the girl unfound
in any way that mattered, Voss still buried
in the town's short memory like a well
run dry. But I remember how it felt—
that instant of impossible ascent,
the wish still burning somewhere in the dark,
too small to matter, much too bright to fade.
outputs.L5:
# The Strength of Steel

Steel is one of humanity's most transformative materials. That combination of iron and carbon, refined through centuries of metallurgical innovation, has shaped civilizations in ways few other substances have matched.

The properties that make steel so valuable are remarkable. Its strength-to-weight ratio allows engineers to construct towering skyscrapers and sweeping bridges that seemed impossible in earlier eras. That same durability makes it essential for everything from surgical instruments to massive industrial machinery.

The history of steel production tells a story of human ingenuity. Ancient blacksmiths discovered that heating iron with carbon-rich materials could produce a harder, more resilient metal. That early knowledge, though rudimentary by modern standards, laid the groundwork for the industrial revolution centuries later. The Bessemer process, developed in the 19th century, transformed steel from a rare, expensive material into something that could be mass-produced affordably.

Today, steel remains indispensable. The construction industry relies on it for structural frameworks. The automotive sector depends on it for vehicle bodies and components. That versatility extends to countless other applications—from kitchen appliances to medical devices, from railway tracks to wind turbines.

What makes steel particularly fascinating is its recyclability. Unlike many materials that degrade in quality when recycled, steel can be melted down and reformed repeatedly without losing its essential properties. That characteristic makes it one of the most sustainable materials available, with recycling rates far exceeding those of plastics or many other metals.

The future of steel continues to evolve. Researchers are developing new alloys that offer greater strength, corrosion resistance, and environmental friendliness. That ongoing innovation ensures steel will remain central to construction, manufacturing, and technology for generations to come. The story of steel is, in many ways, the story of modern civilization itself—a testament to human creativity and our ability to transform raw materials into the foundations of progress.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about oil pumpjacks in a desert landscape near the Pacific, weaving in childhood memory and a discovered body.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Pumpjacks Know

The nodding donkeys work all night,
their iron necks bowing to something
underground and patient,
that same rhythm my father called *the heartbeat of the valley*
when I was young enough to believe
machines could love the earth back.

We drove past them on the way to the coast,
Highway 33 unspooling through Maricopa,
through heat that made the asphalt swim,
and I'd count the pumpjacks like sheep—
one, two, forty-three—
each one dipping its head
in a slow, eternal yes,
yes, yes, yes,
until the ocean finally opened
gray and enormous beyond the last ridge.

*Look*, my father would say,
*that's oil older than the dinosaurs,
older than God's second thought.*

I didn't know yet
what the ground could keep.

Twenty years later I am back
walking an access road at dawn
where sagebrush gives way to gravel,
where someone has left a jacket
folded too carefully over a fence post,
and further on, past the tank battery,
past the smell of crude like a struck match,
a shape in the dry wash
that used to be someone's brother, someone's
countable thing,
the way I once counted pumpjacks
without asking what they lifted,
without asking what the valley
had learned to swallow.

The machines don't stop.
They don't know the difference
between oil and whatever else
sinks slow enough to become
part of the story.

Somewhere the Pacific keeps arriving
and retreating, arriving
and retreating, that same tidal yes,
and here the pumpjacks nod
their black amens
over the body,
over the childhood
I didn't know I'd buried
in the sand-colored hills,

the two of us learning
too late
what patience really costs—

how the earth keeps every secret
we hand it,
how it rocks each one
so gently
into the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a haunting narrative poem set in an oil field where a child rides a pumpjack, and something tragic unfolds nearby.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Rocking Horse Fields

The pumpjacks nod like grazing beasts
across the flatland, rust and bone,
where Daddy works the graveyard shift
and I am nine and left alone

to wander where the derricks creak,
their iron heads bowed low, then high—
a rhythm slow as sleeping lungs,
a metronome beneath the sky.

I called it Horse. I climbed its back
where the counterweight hung, still and wide,
and rode the dip, the rise, the dip,
my hands gripped tight to metal hide.

*Rock me down to where the black gold sleeps,
rock me up to touch the burning sky,
Daddy says the earth has secrets deep,
Daddy says the wildcatters never die—*

They just go under, join the dark,
become the thing that fuels the flame.
I didn't understand it then,
that tragedy could wear Dad's name.

The foreman's truck kicked up the dust
before the sirens found our road.
I was still riding, still counting time,
still trusting what the pumpjack showed—

that rising follows every fall,
that dark gives way to light again—
but they pulled him from the casing pipe
too still, too slow, too far from when

I'd waved that morning, half-asleep,
not knowing it would be the last.
The horse kept rocking, kept its time,
indifferent to the men rushed past.

*Rock me down to where the black gold sleeps,
rock me up though the sky won't hold you,
Daddy said the earth has secrets deep—
now the earth keeps Daddy's secrets, too.*

I ride it still, in dreams, at night,
that patient beast with the iron spine,
and somewhere in its endless nod
I hear him breathing, out of time—

not gone, but folded into ground,
pressed like fern-print into stone,
another layer in the black
that rises up through pipe and bone,

through fires lit in far-off rooms,
through engines coughing on the road—
my father, burning, mile by mile,
lighting up the world he showed

me from the back of rusted Horse,
who rocks forever, who does not grieve,
who only knows the pull and give,
the taking that the earth receives.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that uses "steel horses" as a metaphor for oil pumps, incorporating themes of death, memory, and coastal wildfire imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# Steel Horses

Along the bluffs where sage once burned green
the steel horses bow and rise, bow and rise,
their iron necks dipping into the earth's
old wounds, drinking what the dead left buried—

sunlight trapped in Jurassic shadow,
ferns and reptiles pressed to oil,
memory compressed to fuel.

They do not tire, these horses.
They do not sweat or foam or fall.
They nod like mourners at a grave
that never closes, never fills,
counting seconds with their heads.

Somewhere past the ridge, the real fire comes—
not the slow burn locked in rock
but the fast one, orange and hungry,
eating chaparral and eucalyptus,
turning coastal fog to smoke,
turning morning into amber dusk.

The horses do not run from it.
They cannot run. They only nod,
even as ash falls like grey snow
on their patient iron spines,
even as the hills that held them
turn to embers, turn to bone-white ridges,
turn to something like a memory themselves.

We built them to remember for us—
to draw the deep past upward, burn it,
scatter it as heat and light and smoke
that drifts out toward the same sea
that once, millennia ago,
buried these fields in silence,
in sediment, in time.

Now the pumps keep nodding
through the burning season,
mechanical, patient, blind,
drawing dead light from dead ground
while the living hills catch fire
and the living forget
what a horse once was—

before it was steel,
before it was bowing to nothing
but the ground, the ground,
the endless asking of the ground.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical, image-heavy poem about growing up near oil derricks, blending innocence, danger, and loss across different points in time.
counterfactuals.output:
# Signal Hill

**I. Before**

The pumpjacks nodded like patient horses
grazing on something older than us,
their black heads bowing, rising, bowing—
a rosary counted in crude and rust.
We rode our bikes between the metal ribs,
found arrowheads and rattlesnake skins,
called the tanks *the moons* because they gleamed
white and swollen against the bruise-dark hills.

Someone's father worked the derricks then,
came home smelling of diesel and thunder,
his hands two maps of continents
we couldn't read but loved to hold.

**II. The Middle Years**

Summer, 1987. Sixteen and reckless,
we'd climb the chain-link where it sagged,
dare each other toward the flare stacks
burning orange against the bruised horizon—
that fire that never seemed to sleep,
some god's eternal, hungry eye.

Danny Cortez kissed me once
beneath a derrick's skeleton shadow,
tasted like smoke and stolen beer,
and for a moment I believed
the whole earth hummed for us alone,
that oil was just the blood of something
patient, waiting to be born.

**III. What the Ground Remembers**

The accident took two men in '92—
I don't say their names, but the town does,
folds them into evening conversation
like a prayer you say without thinking.
After that, the derricks looked different:
not horses now, but crows,
black wings folded, waiting, waiting.

My father's hands grew stiller.
The maps in them turned to scar tissue,
lines that led nowhere but backward.

**IV. Now**

I drive past what's left—
half the field capped and quiet,
pumpjacks rusted mid-nod
like a sentence someone forgot to finish.
The new houses climb the hill
where we once hunted arrowheads,
their beige facades indifferent
to what still sleeps beneath the concrete.

Sometimes at dusk I see the ghost of flame,
the flare stack's orange tongue
licking a sky that no longer notices,
and I am sixteen again, unkissed,
believing in a fire that would not fail us,
believing the ground beneath our feet
was only sleeping, only patient,
not already grieving
what it would become.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, melancholic poem that moves between a boy's dare on an oil pump, a missing girl's discovery, a man's suicide, and a firefly wish, ending with fire in the hills.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Pumpjack Remembers**

The boy climbed the pumpjack at midnight,
dared by nothing but the moon's slow eye,
and the machine breathed under him
like something buried that still dreamed of walking.
He counted ten. He counted the dark
counting back. Below, the fields lay open
as a mouth that had said the same word
for forty years and forgotten its meaning.

Somewhere past the fence line, dogs found her—
the missing girl, curled where the grass gave up,
her shoes still tied, as if she'd meant
to keep walking through whatever door
had opened in the dirt. No one screamed.
The finding was too quiet for that,
just men standing in a loose circle
the way you stand around a fire
that has already gone out.

The man who chose the river
did it on a Tuesday, which seemed wrong—
Tuesdays should be safe, should smell of coffee
and small errands. He left his boots
on the bank, pointed toward town,
as if his feet had decided to stay
a little longer than the rest of him.
The water didn't pause. It never does.
It just kept telling its one long story
to whoever would still listen.

A child, elsewhere, in a yard gone soft with dusk,
cupped a firefly and made a wish
she wouldn't remember by morning—
something about her mother staying,
something about the dark not being
the same shape as an ending.
The insect blinked in her palm
like a small machine misfiring hope,
then lifted, unkeepable,
into the larger dark that keeps
everything it's given.

And the boy on the pumpjack held on
past ten, past the dare, past the moon's
indifferent witnessing, until the metal
groaned beneath him like a throat
remembering song.

By then the hills had already caught—
some spark, some carelessness, some old wound
finally opening its mouth to speak—
and the horizon wore its orange grief
the way the dead wear silence:
completely, without apology,

lighting the fields where she was found,
the river where he left his shoes,
the yard where wishes rise and die
mid-air, and the boy climbing down
finally, slowly, into a world
that has already decided
what it means to burn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
